 Columns | 23 hours ago Cosmetics and personal care industry as a component of export basket
 Nilratan Halder
 Published :
 Oct 29, 2026, 18:21 
 At a time when Bangladesh is exploring its prospects for diversifying the export basket beyond the readymade garments, its cosmetics industry has great potential. This observation is not made by any ordinary mortal but by Dr. Kim Junoh, a leading South Korean cosmetics scientist. With long experience in skincare formulations, he has of late joined the Skin'O and Coslab Personal Care Limited in Bangladesh as a consultant to expedite collaboration between researchers in Dhaka and Seoul. Skin'O has been producing skincare products after the K-beauty model. This Korean brand of skincare products is enjoying global demands. 
 Detractors may dismiss the proposal for development of the cosmetics industry. But here is a sector that compares well with the leather industry. The global cosmetics market is worth between US$354.68 and $375.62 billion in 2026. But the broader beauty and personal care industry is valued approximately at $635 to 754.37 billion. Against these figures, the global leather and leather goods industry is projected to be worth $566.23 billion in 2026. In terms of expansion outlooks, though, the leather industry in the world is likely to grow to $982.42 billion by 2034 while the beauty and personal care industry may reach $876 billion by the year 2031. Different organisations and study agencies, however, have come up with different estimates.
 According to the Grand View Research, the global beauty and personal care industry is valued at $693.9 billion in 2026 and is likely to reach $1,181.6 billion by 2033 at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 7.9 per cent. The Statista Market Forecast maintains the market to be $754.37 billion in 2026 and likely to grow at a 3.71 CAGR through 2031. The Euromonitor International values this market at $647 billion on the basis of a 2.5 per cent growth rate. Emerging markets are driving the cosmetics and beauty care growth.
 The global market value of beauty and personal care is higher than that of the leather and footwear industry according to estimates and projections by all the agencies concerned. But apart from one, the other monitoring agencies put the CAGRs lower than the global leather industry's growth. Yet there is good reason to share the optimism expressed by Dr. Kim Junoh. L'Oreal of France is the most celebrated brand of cosmetics and personal care products in the world. Procter and Gamble (P&G), Unilever, Chanel, NIVEA, Gillette follow it. Of course, there are other quality products produced primarily by companies in Europe and America. In Asia, Japan and South Korea have lately made their presence felt in the niche market.
 According to Dr. Kim, K-beauty products have become quite popular across the world. Now his guidance and active involvement with Skin'O can raise the quality of local cosmetics and personal care products here. The fact that local products are used by economically constrained segments of people is undeniable. But the middle and upper classes of society look for foreign brands. Over the past two years, import of foreign brands of cosmetics and grooming products has been severely limited raising the prices abnormally. This offers a good opportunity for improving the quality of domestic products.
 The prospects of higher domestic demand and export highlight the need for paying greater attention to developing the sector to a level where it can produce world-class cosmetics and beauty products. On this score, the Korean expert's opinion counts highly. His experience in formulations and innovation will prove a valuable asset in spurring production and quality. To that end, there is no alternative to developing a broader base of this industry. Infrastructure development and investment by more companies can lead to a competitive regime for desirable quality enhancement.
 This can happen if scientific research with new ingredients is carried on and improved technology applied to complement the effort. Many of the raw materials are likely to be available locally. If the knowledge and experience of men like Dr. Kim can be used for the purpose, there is no reason why the cosmetics and beauty care industry will not flourish in this country. The most important issue is to ensure the quality of products. Once this aspect is taken care of, the next task is promotion of products and access to the market dominated by western brands.
 Readymade garments from Bangladesh had to go through such an arduous process and if cosmetics and beauty products meet the quality benchmark, this sector can gradually earn a reasonable market share for itself. Primarily, it can direct focus to markets in Asia, Africa and Latin America. Low-cost production can be a clinching factor for a significant price gap with products of the established companies and brands. Bangladesh will also vie for international recognition of its own brands. In this context, Dr. Kim's experience and strategy may prove valuable. 
 Already, the small and medium enterprises of the country have set their eyes on producing spare parts and precision components of cars and other vehicles. Production of cosmetics and beauty products can as well be a viable option for some of these enterprises. In that case, there will be a need for extensive technical training for the workforce before setting up production units. Under a comprehensive plan, short-term and long-term goals should be set for the sector to achieve.
